---
title: "Reference Implementations: multinma, mlumr, and uitc"
---

## Purpose and scope {#sec-impl-scope}

The preceding thirty chapters built the mathematics of indirect treatment comparison from linear algebra
to machine-checked proof. This appendix is the bridge to computation. It maps the objects the book
*defines and proves* onto the functions, arguments, and Stan model files that *evaluate* them in three R
packages: `multinma` for multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) on connected networks
[@phillippo2020mlnmr], `mlumr` for multilevel unanchored meta-regression (ML-UMR) on disconnected
two-treatment evidence [@chandler2025mlumr], and `uitc`, an umbrella for unanchored
population-adjusted indirect comparison (PAIC) that bundles matching-adjusted indirect comparison
(MAIC), simulated treatment comparison (STC), a doubly-robust estimator, and quantitative bias analysis
(QBA). All three estimate their Bayesian models in Stan [@carpenter2017stan].

This is a map, not a tutorial. Code is kept to the minimum needed to locate each mathematical object in
the software; the package vignettes are the place to learn the workflows end to end. Symbols follow
[Notation](/notation.qmd) throughout: $\eta_{ijk}$ is the linear predictor, $g^{-1}$ the inverse link,
$\theta_{ijk}=g^{-1}(\eta_{ijk})$ the conditional mean on the outcome scale, $f_j$ the covariate density
in study $j$, $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ its mean and covariance, and $d_{ab(\mathcal{P})}$
the marginal relative effect of $b$ versus $a$ in target population $\mathcal{P}$.

::: {.remark}
The correspondence in this appendix is at the level of mathematical object, not source line. Package
versions move; the function signatures shown were read from `multinma`, `mlumr`, and `uitc` at the time
of writing and may drift. What does not drift is the underlying mathematics: each computational object
named below implements a specific definition, equation, or theorem proved in the chapters, and that
linkage is what the tables record. Where a formula is reproduced here it is reproduced exactly; verify
argument names against the installed help pages before relying on them.
:::

## Orientation for the first-time reader {#sec-impl-orientation}

Read this appendix *alongside* the chapters, not instead of them. Each chapter answers *why* a method is
built the way it is and *proves* that it works; this appendix answers *where* that mathematics lives in
the software and *which* function evaluates it. The intended use is lookup and verification: when you have
read the aggregation theorem of Chapter 20 and want to see the line of Stan that computes it, or when you
are about to call `nma()` and want to know which equation each argument controls, this is the page to
open. A few subsections (the Stan-file inventories, the adjusted-binomial reparametrization) are there
mainly for readers checking that the code faithfully implements the proofs; a first-time user can skim
them and return later. Everything else is meant to be read on a first pass.

If you are new to these methods, a good order is: read this orientation, choose your package from the
decision guide in @sec-impl-which-package, read that package's pipeline table, and follow the prose
pointers back into the chapters whenever a term or symbol is unfamiliar. The three object-to-code maps
(@sec-impl-multinma-map, @sec-impl-mlumr-map, @sec-impl-uitc-map) are the reference cards to return to
once you know the workflow.

::: {.remark}
**A running example, used throughout.** To keep the symbols attached to something concrete, we carry one
small scenario through the appendix. The outcome is a binary treatment response (PASI 75, meaning at
least a 75 percent reduction in a psoriasis severity score at week 12: `1` if achieved, `0` if not). The
covariates are patient `age` in years (continuous) and `sex` (binary, coded `1` for female). Three
treatments appear: drug `A`, our new treatment, for which we hold individual patient data (IPD, one row
per patient); drug `B`, a competitor, for which we have only a published aggregate summary (mean age,
percent female, and responders out of total); and placebo `P`, a possible common comparator. The goal is
the relative effect of `A` versus `B` in a decision target population with mean age 48 and 40 percent
female. Two data situations recur:

- *Connected (anchored) network:* trial 1 reports IPD on `A` versus `P`; trial 2 reports aggregate data
  (AgD) on `B` versus `P`. They share the placebo arm `P`, so the network is *connected* and the `A`
  versus `B` contrast is *anchored* through `P`. This is the `multinma` setting.
- *Disconnected (unanchored) network:* trial 1 reports IPD on `A`, trial 2 reports AgD on `B`, and the
  two share no common arm. The network is *disconnected*, the contrast is *unanchored*, and it is
  identified only by adjusting the IPD to the comparator population. This is the `mlumr` and `uitc`
  setting.
:::

Two words recur and decide everything below, so fix them here. An *anchored* comparison estimates `A`
versus `B` indirectly through a shared reference arm that both trials contain (in the example, placebo
`P`); the shared arm cancels study-level nuisance terms, which is why a connected network can be analyzed
with the trial-level contrasts of Chapter 14 and Chapter 15. An *unanchored* comparison has no shared
arm, so nothing cancels; the entire between-study difference in outcomes must be explained by adjusting
for covariates, a much stronger assumption (Chapter 12, Chapter 26). Whenever the appendix says
"anchored" or "unanchored" it means exactly this.

### Which package answers which question {#sec-impl-which-package}

Choose the package from the shape of your evidence, not from the method name. The rule is the network
structure, summarized here and repeated as a routing table in @sec-impl-together.

| Your situation (running example) | Network | Method | Package |
|---|---|---|---|
| IPD on `A` vs `P`, AgD on `B` vs `P`, shared arm `P` | connected, anchored | ML-NMR | `multinma` |
| IPD on `A`, AgD on `B`, no shared arm | disconnected, unanchored | ML-UMR | `mlumr` |
| Same unanchored data, but you also want MAIC, STC, doubly-robust, and a bias analysis side by side | unanchored | PAIC and QBA | `uitc` |

In health-technology-assessment (HTA) terms, the three packages answer three versions of the same
submission question, "what is the effect of our drug `A` versus competitor `B` in the population our
decision is about?"

- **`multinma` (ML-NMR).** You have at least one IPD trial and the network of trials is connected through
  shared treatments. You want the anchored `A` versus `B` effect, transported to a chosen target
  population. Reach for `multinma`. This is the statistically strongest situation, because the shared arm
  protects you.
- **`mlumr` (ML-UMR).** Your IPD trial and the competitor's trial share no arm, so the network is broken.
  You must lean entirely on covariate adjustment to bridge the gap. Reach for `mlumr`, and expect to
  defend the adjustment assumptions carefully, because there is no anchor to fall back on.
- **`uitc` (PAIC plus QBA).** The same broken network, but you want to run the established
  population-adjustment methods (MAIC, STC), a doubly-robust combination, and a quantitative bias analysis
  on one data object, so you can report an estimate next to its sensitivity analysis. Reach for `uitc`.

### What data each method needs {#sec-impl-data-needed}

Before any of these calls will run, the data must be in a specific shape. The following table answers the
practical question "what do I need in hand?" Details of each field appear with the relevant pipeline
below.

| Method (package) | Network | IPD needed | AgD outcome summary | Covariate summary | Survival input | Main output |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ML-NMR (`multinma`) | connected | one row per patient: study, treatment, outcome, covariates | per arm: responders `r` and arm size `n` (or mean and standard error) | for each AgD covariate: a distribution, e.g. mean and standard deviation, or a proportion | KM curve digitized to pseudo-IPD via `set_agd_surv()` | anchored contrasts and transported marginal effects |
| ML-UMR (`mlumr`) | disconnected | one row per patient on index treatment `A`: outcome, covariates | comparator `B` only: responders and total (or mean, standard error) | comparator covariate means, and a type per covariate (`continuous`/`binary`) | digitized KM curve for `B` via `set_agd_surv()` | unanchored marginal `A` vs `B` effect in each population |
| MAIC (`uitc`) | disconnected | index `A` IPD: outcome, covariates | comparator `B` outcome summary | comparator covariate *means* to match | (as `mlumr`) | weighted effect, effective sample size, balance diagnostics |
| STC (`uitc`/`mlumr`) | disconnected | index `A` IPD: outcome, covariates | comparator `B` outcome summary | comparator covariate means (and covariance if simulating) | (as `mlumr`) | G-computation effect |
| Doubly-robust (`uitc`) | disconnected | index `A` IPD: outcome, covariates | comparator `B` outcome summary | comparator covariate means and covariance | not applicable | doubly-robust effect with bootstrap interval |
| QBA (`uitc`) | any | the fitted estimate and its inputs | as for the base method | as for the base method, plus a hypothesized unmeasured covariate | as for the base method | E-value, tipping point, or probabilistic bias interval |

### Terms used in this appendix {#sec-impl-glossary}

Every term here is defined and used in the chapters; this table is a one-line reminder so the appendix
reads without flipping back. Each row points to the chapter that develops it.

| Term | One-line meaning | Developed in |
|---|---|---|
| IPD, AgD | individual patient data (one row per patient) versus aggregate data (per-arm summaries) | Chapter 17 |
| anchored / unanchored | with / without a shared reference arm linking the two treatments | Chapter 14, Chapter 26 |
| connected / disconnected network | the trials do / do not form one linked graph of shared treatments | Chapter 15, Chapter 16 |
| effect modifier (EM) | a covariate that changes the *treatment effect*, so it must be balanced across populations | Chapter 11 |
| prognostic variable (PV) | a covariate that predicts *outcome* regardless of treatment | Chapter 11 |
| SPFA | shared prognostic factor assumption: prognostic effects are the same under both treatments | Chapter 26 |
| SEMA | shared effect modifier assumption: effect-modifier interactions are shared across studies | Chapter 17 |
| conditional effect | a contrast for patients with fixed covariate values (a within-subgroup effect) | Chapter 11, Chapter 23 |
| marginal effect | a contrast averaged over a whole target population | Chapter 11, Chapter 23 |
| collapsible / non-collapsible | whether the marginal effect equals the average of conditional effects on that scale | Chapter 11 |
| G-computation | fit the outcome model on IPD, then average its predictions over a target covariate distribution | Chapter 19 |
| effective sample size (ESS) | the equivalent number of unweighted patients after weighting, $(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2$ | Chapter 18 |
| QMC | quasi-Monte Carlo, a low-discrepancy grid used to average a model over a covariate distribution | Chapter 22 |

## multinma: multilevel network meta-regression {#sec-impl-multinma}

`multinma` fits the ML-NMR model of Chapters 20 to 25: one individual-level regression
$$
g\big(\theta_{ijk}\big)=\eta_{ijk}=\mu_j+\boldsymbol{\beta}_1^\top\mathbf{x}_{ij}+\big(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}^\top\mathbf{x}_{ij}+\gamma_k\big)
$$ {#eq-impl-mlnmr-model}
shared across a *connected* network, fitted to individual patient data (IPD) directly and to aggregate
data (AgD) through the aggregation integral. The package is the reference implementation accompanying
@phillippo2020mlnmr and its survival extension @phillippo2025general.

Read @eq-impl-mlnmr-model one term at a time; it is the whole model, and every `multinma` argument sets
one of its pieces. The left side $g(\theta_{ijk})$ is the response of patient $i$ in study $j$ on
treatment $k$, mapped to the linear-predictor scale by the link $g$ (for a binary outcome $g$ is the
logit, so $\eta_{ijk}$ is a log-odds). The right side builds that log-odds from four parts.

| Term | Name | What it does (running example) | `multinma` |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mu_j$ | study baseline | the outcome level in study $j$'s control arm; a separate intercept per trial | fitted per study automatically |
| $\boldsymbol{\beta}_1^\top\mathbf{x}_{ij}$ | prognostic effects | how age and sex shift outcome *regardless of treatment* | main effects added via `regression =` |
| $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}^\top\mathbf{x}_{ij}$ | effect modification | how age and sex shift the *treatment* effect of arm $k$ | the `:.trt` interaction in `regression =` |
| $\gamma_k$ | treatment effect | the effect of treatment $k$ versus the network reference, at the reference covariate values | the treatment coefficients |

In words: a patient's modeled log-odds of response is their study's baseline, plus a prognostic shift for
being older or female, plus (only on an active arm) an effect-modifying shift and the drug's own effect.
The single most important feature is that *the same* $\boldsymbol{\beta}_1$, $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}$,
and $\gamma_k$ are shared across every study in the network; that sharing is what lets an IPD trial and an
AgD trial inform one regression, and it is licensed by the shared-effect-modifier assumption (SEMA) of
Chapter 17. When a covariate modifies the effect (its $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}$ is nonzero), the `A`
versus `B` contrast genuinely depends on the population's age and sex mix, which is the entire reason
population adjustment is needed.

### The pipeline {#sec-impl-multinma-pipeline}

Six functions carry an analysis from data to fitted model. Each one realizes a construction from the
book.

| Function | Mathematical role |
|---|---|
| `set_ipd()` | Register an IPD study: rows are individuals, with outcome and covariates entering @eq-impl-mlnmr-model directly. |
| `set_agd_arm()` | Register an arm-based AgD study: summary outcomes per arm, to be matched by the aggregation integral (@thm-aggregation). |
| `set_agd_contrast()` | Register a contrast-based AgD study: relative effects with a covariance, the meta-analytic likelihood of Chapter 13. |
| `set_agd_surv()` | Register AgD with reconstructed survival data (Kaplan-Meier curves digitized to pseudo-IPD), the general-likelihood survival branch of Chapter 25. |
| `combine_network()` | Assemble the registered studies into one network object; checks connectivity (the precondition removed only in Chapter 26). |
| `add_integration()` | Attach quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) integration points to every AgD study (Chapter 22). |
| `nma()` | Build the Stan data, choose the likelihood and link, and sample the posterior (Chapter 24). |

Before any of this runs, the data must be in the shape those functions expect: IPD is one row per
patient, arm-based AgD is one row per arm. For the running example the two inputs look like this (a few
rows shown; the column names are what matter).

```r
# ipd_data: one row per patient in the IPD trial of A vs P
  study    trt   r  age  sex
  Trial1     P   0   52    0
  Trial1     A   1   47    1
  Trial1     A   0   61    0
# ... one row per patient ...

# agd_data: one row per arm in the AgD trial of B vs P
  study    trt    r    n  age_mean  age_sd  sex_prop
  Trial2     P   58  200      49.1    11.8      0.42
  Trial2     B   96  201      48.6    12.1      0.39
```

Here `r` is the outcome column (a responder indicator `1`/`0` per patient in IPD, a responder *count* per
arm in AgD), `n` is the arm size, `study` and `trt` are the study and treatment labels, and the `age_*`
and `sex_prop` columns are the covariate summaries the AgD trial publishes. The canonical call sequence is

```r
net <- combine_network(
  set_ipd(ipd_data, study, trt, r = r),
  set_agd_arm(agd_data, study, trt, r = r, n = n)
)
net <- add_integration(net, age = distr(qnorm, mean = age_mean, sd = age_sd),
                            sex = distr(qbern, prob = sex_prop), n_int = 64L)
fit <- nma(net, regression = ~ (age + sex):.trt, likelihood = "bernoulli2",
           link = "logit", trt_effects = "fixed")
```

The regression formula `~ (age + sex):.trt` encodes the effect-modifier interactions
$\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}$; the special term `.trt` is the treatment factor. Prognostic main effects
$\boldsymbol{\beta}_1$ are added automatically with `center = TRUE`.

Each argument of that call controls one modeling choice. In ordinary trial language:

| Argument | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| `study`, `trt` | the columns naming the study and the treatment arm |
| `r = r` | set the model's responder input to the data column named `r`; the left `r` is the fixed argument name, the right `r` is your column name |
| `n = n` | the arm size column (AgD only; IPD has one patient per row) |
| `regression = ~ (age + sex):.trt` | which covariates are effect modifiers; `.trt` is the placeholder for the treatment factor, so `(age + sex):.trt` means "let age and sex modify the treatment effect" |
| `likelihood = "bernoulli2"` | the outcome family; `bernoulli2` is the two-parameter binary likelihood of @sec-impl-multinma-aggregation |
| `link = "logit"` | the link $g$; `logit` makes $\eta$ a log-odds |
| `trt_effects = "fixed"` | fixed-effect (common-effect) treatment effects, one $\gamma_k$ shared across studies, as opposed to `"random"` for treatment effects that vary by study |

The note that main effects are added "with `center = TRUE`" means the covariates are centered before
entering the model, so that the treatment coefficients $\gamma_k$ read as effects *at the average
covariate values of the network*, not at age zero. Centering does not change the fitted contrasts in any
target population; it only fixes what the raw $\gamma_k$ mean and improves the sampler's geometry. Which
population the final estimand refers to is set later, by `relative_effects()` and `marginal_effects()`
(@sec-impl-multinma-estimand), not by centering.

### The aggregation integral {#sec-impl-multinma-aggregation}

Start with the reason this section exists. The obvious way to predict an aggregate arm's response rate is
to plug the arm's *mean* covariates into the fitted model: evaluate $g^{-1}$ at mean age and percent
female. For any nonlinear link (a logit, a log) this is *wrong*, and Chapter 20 proves it is wrong; the
error is @thm-aggregation-bias. Averaging a curved function is not the same as the function of the
average. So `multinma` never does that; instead it averages *patient-level* predictions, which is the
content of @thm-aggregation.

Concretely, the correct aggregate-level mean is the *average of the inverse-linked individual means*, not
the inverse link of the average linear predictor. For an arm $k$ in AgD study $j$,
$$
\bar\theta_{jk}=\int_{\mathcal{X}} g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})\big)\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
\;\approx\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{m=1}^{N} g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}^{(m)})\big),
\qquad \mathbf{x}^{(m)}\sim f_j ,
$$ {#eq-impl-aggregation}
which is @eq-agg-aggregate-mean evaluated at the $N$ integration points of @sec-impl-multinma-qmc. Read
the right side as a recipe: generate $N$ synthetic patients whose covariates follow the AgD study's
reported distribution $f_j$, predict each one's response probability from the shared regression, then
average those probabilities. That average, not the prediction at the average patient, is what the arm's
observed responder count is matched to. In `inst/stan/binomial_1par.stan` this is the single line (the
comments are ours)

```stan
// theta_agd_arm_ii stacks every arm's N per-patient predicted probabilities end to end.
// This slice pulls out the block belonging to AgD arm i, then averages it: exactly the integral above.
theta_agd_arm_bar[i] = mean(theta_agd_arm_ii[(1 + (i-1)*nint):(i*nint)]);
// "~" is Stan's sampling statement (a likelihood contribution, not an assignment):
// the observed responder count is binomial with size n and the integrated probability.
agd_arm_r ~ binomial(agd_arm_n, theta_agd_arm_bar);
```

where `theta_agd_arm_ii` holds the $N$ values $g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}^{(m)}))$ and `nint` is $N$.
(The index arithmetic `(1 + (i-1)*nint):(i*nint)` is just "rows $(i-1)N+1$ through $iN$," the contiguous
block for the $i$-th arm in a stacked array.)

The two-parameter file `binomial_2par.stan` refines the likelihood, and the reason is a variance mismatch
worth spelling out. The aggregate arm is a *mixture*: the model assigns patients with different covariates
different response probabilities $\theta_m$, so summarizing the arm by the single number $\bar\theta_{jk}$
discards the spread of those probabilities. A plain binomial with probability $\bar\theta_{jk}$ ignores
that spread and can understate the dispersion. The first two moments of the per-patient probabilities are
$$
\bar\theta_{jk}=\frac1N\sum_m\theta_m,\qquad \overline{\theta^2}_{jk}=\frac1N\sum_m\theta_m^2,
$$
and their gap $\overline{\theta^2}_{jk}-\bar\theta_{jk}^{\,2}\ge 0$ is precisely the variance of those
probabilities (zero only if every patient has the same $\theta$). To carry that extra dispersion while
keeping the same mean, `binomial_2par.stan` matches both moments with an adjusted binomial,
$$
n'_{jk}=n_{jk}\,\frac{\bar\theta_{jk}^{\,2}}{\overline{\theta^2}_{jk}},
\qquad
p'_{jk}=\frac{\overline{\theta^2}_{jk}}{\bar\theta_{jk}},
\qquad\text{so that } n'_{jk}\,p'_{jk}=n_{jk}\,\bar\theta_{jk},
$$ {#eq-impl-adjusted-binomial}
which preserves the integrated mean $n_{jk}\bar\theta_{jk}$ (the product $n'p'$ is unchanged) while using
$p'_{jk}=\overline{\theta^2}_{jk}/\bar\theta_{jk}\ge\bar\theta_{jk}$ to widen the variance toward the
mixture's. This is the implementation of the aggregate likelihood @eq-agg-aggregate-likelihood. Contrast
all of this with the *naive* plug-in $g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_j))$ of @eq-agg-naive, whose bias
@thm-aggregation-bias quantifies; `multinma` never forms the naive quantity for a nonlinear link.

### Quasi-Monte Carlo integration {#sec-impl-multinma-qmc}

Here is the practical problem this machinery solves. A published trial almost never releases its
patients' covariates; it reports summaries, a mean age, a standard deviation, a percent female, sometimes
a correlation. To evaluate the aggregation integral @eq-impl-aggregation we nonetheless need a *cloud of
covariate profiles* that reproduces those summaries. `add_integration()` manufactures exactly that: a grid
of $N$ synthetic covariate vectors whose marginal distributions and correlations match the reported
summaries, so that averaging model predictions across the grid approximates averaging over the real (but
unpublished) patient distribution. "Quasi-Monte Carlo" (QMC) just means the grid is a cleverly spread
low-discrepancy set rather than random draws, which makes the average converge faster.

`add_integration()` builds the points $\{\mathbf{x}^{(m)}\}_{m=1}^N$ that turn @eq-impl-aggregation into a
finite sum. It implements the pipeline of Chapter 22: a Sobol' net (@def-sobol-net) pushed through a
Gaussian copula (@def-gaussian-copula) and the marginal quantile functions (@thm-inverse-cdf),
$$
\mathbf{x}^{(m)}=\Big(F_{j,1}^{-1}\big(u_1^{(m)}\big),\dots,F_{j,d}^{-1}\big(u_d^{(m)}\big)\Big),
\qquad
u_q^{(m)}=\Phi\!\big((L\,\mathbf{z}^{(m)})_q\big),\quad
\mathbf{z}^{(m)}=\Phi^{-1}\!\big(\mathbf{a}^{(m)}\big),
$$ {#eq-impl-qmc}
where $\{\mathbf{a}^{(m)}\}\subset[0,1)^d$ is the Sobol' sequence and $LL^\top=\Omega$ is the Cholesky
factor of the copula correlation matrix (this is @eq-qmc-pipeline). Written as nested transformations the
display is dense, so read it as a four-step pipeline, each step feeding the next in the order the data
flows.

| Step | Transformation | Produces | Set by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. spread | $\mathbf{a}^{(m)}\in[0,1)^d$, a Sobol' low-discrepancy point | an evenly spread point in the unit cube | `n_int` (how many points $N$) |
| 2. to normal scores | $\mathbf{z}^{(m)}=\Phi^{-1}(\mathbf{a}^{(m)})$ | independent standard-normal coordinates | (internal) |
| 3. correlate, back to uniform | $u_q^{(m)}=\Phi\big((L\mathbf{z}^{(m)})_q\big)$, with $LL^\top=\Omega$ | correlated uniforms with the target dependence | `cor`, `cor_adjust` (build $\Omega$, then $L$) |
| 4. to covariate scale | $x_q^{(m)}=F_{j,q}^{-1}(u_q^{(m)})$ | a synthetic patient's covariate values | `<cov> = distr(qfun, ...)` (the marginal $F_{j,q}^{-1}$) |

The Gaussian copula (step 3) is the device that lets us glue *arbitrary* marginal distributions (age
maybe normal, a biomarker maybe skewed) together with a *chosen* correlation: it imposes the dependence
in a normal latent space, then maps each coordinate back to its own marginal in step 4. If the copula is
new to you, read it as "a correlation structure applied to uniforms, so any marginals can be attached
afterward," and see the picture in Chapter 22. The pieces map to arguments as follows.

| Argument of `add_integration()` | Mathematical object |
|---|---|
| `<cov> = distr(qfun, ...)` | the marginal quantile function $F_{j,q}^{-1}$ of covariate $q$ (`distr` wraps a base-R `q*` function). |
| `n_int` | the number of integration points $N$; error decays like $N^{-1}(\log N)^d$ by Koksma-Hlawka (@thm-koksma-hlawka), beating the $N^{-1/2}$ Monte Carlo rate (@cor-tensor-quadrature-curse). |
| `cor` | the input covariate correlation matrix used to build $\Omega$. |
| `cor_adjust` | the rule converting `cor` (Spearman or Pearson) to the Gaussian-copula correlation $\Omega$ (Sklar's theorem, @thm-sklar). |

The `distr()` wrapper deserves a word, since it appears with no introduction in the call above.
`distr(qfun, ...)` bundles a base-R quantile function with its parameters into the marginal
$F_{j,q}^{-1}$ that step 4 needs. For instance `distr(qnorm, mean = 48, sd = 12)` represents an age
marginal that is normal with mean 48 and standard deviation 12: given a uniform $u$ it returns
`qnorm(u, mean = 48, sd = 12)`, the age at quantile $u$. Likewise `distr(qbern, prob = 0.40)` encodes a
binary covariate that is female with probability 0.40. You supply one `distr()` per covariate, using the
summaries the AgD trial reported.

How many points? `n_int` is $N$, and 64 is a common default. Because the Koksma-Hlawka rate
(@thm-koksma-hlawka) is roughly $N^{-1}$ up to a log factor that grows with the covariate dimension $d$,
more covariates need more points; the honest way to choose $N$ is empirical. Fit with `n_int = 64L`,
refit with it doubled, and confirm the estimand you care about moves by less than your tolerance;
`plot_integration_error()` automates this check as the empirical analogue of the Koksma-Hlawka bound.
Cost grows linearly in $N$, so doubling the points doubles the integration work, not more.

### The target-population estimand {#sec-impl-multinma-estimand}

A fitted `stan_nma` object stores the conditional parameters $(\mu_j,\boldsymbol{\beta}_1,\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k},\gamma_k)$.
The estimand machinery of Chapter 23 turns these into a contrast in *any* target population, via the
target-population integral @thm-target-population-integral.

Two kinds of answer come out of the same fit, and confusing them is a common error, so fix the
distinction first (if it is unclear, reread Chapter 23 before calling these functions). A *conditional*
effect is for patients with *given* covariates: the `A` versus `B` log-odds ratio for a 55-year-old
woman. A *marginal* effect is *averaged over a whole population*: the `A` versus `B` effect seen across
the entire target population's age and sex mix. On a nonlinear scale such as the odds ratio these differ,
because the odds ratio is non-collapsible (Chapter 11); the population-average effect is not the average
of subgroup effects. For an HTA submission the reported number is almost always the *marginal* effect in
the decision population, since that is the effect a payer would experience in practice. So
`relative_effects()` gives the conditional building blocks, and `marginal_effects()` gives the reportable
population summary.

| Function | Returns | Book object |
|---|---|---|
| `relative_effects()` | conditional contrasts $\delta_{j,\,t_1 t_k}$ in a study or `newdata` population | @eq-mlnmr-est-cond, the conditional estimand of @def-mlnmr-target-contrast |
| `predict()` | absolute outcomes $\bar\theta$ on the response scale (`type = "response"`) in a target population | the population mean of @eq-impl-aggregation in $\mathcal{P}^{*}$ |
| `marginal_effects()` | marginal contrasts $d_{ab(\mathcal{P}^{*})}$ (difference, ratio, or link scale) | @eq-mlnmr-est-marg, the marginal estimand |

In the running example, `relative_effects()` might report a conditional log-odds ratio for `A` versus `B`
of, say, $-0.82$ (95 percent credible interval $-1.21$ to $-0.43$) at the network's average covariates,
`predict(type = "response")` the absolute response probabilities in each arm of the target population, and
`marginal_effects()` the population-averaged `A` versus `B` contrast to put in the submission. (These
numbers are illustrative, not from a real fit.)

Supplying `newdata` (with its own `add_integration()` points) is exactly the change of target population
$\mathcal{P}\mapsto\mathcal{P}^{*}$ that @thm-target-population-integral licenses; with no `newdata` the
estimand defaults to each study's own population. So the *same* fitted model produces different reported
effects for different target populations, and choosing that population is a substantive decision, not a
default.

::: {.remark}
**Sanity check: ML-NMR contains NMA.** When every study is AgD and no covariates enter the regression, the
aggregation integral is trivial and the model collapses to standard network meta-analysis; a call like
`nma(net, trt_effects = "fixed")` with no `regression =` reproduces the Chapter 15 estimator. This is the
computational witness of @thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma, and it is a good first check that a network is set up
correctly: turn off the regression and confirm you recover the familiar NMA result.
:::

### Object-to-code map {#sec-impl-multinma-map}

| Book object | Chapter result | `multinma` |
|---|---|---|
| Individual model @eq-impl-mlnmr-model | @def-individual-model | `nma(regression = ...)` |
| Aggregation integral $\bar\theta_{jk}$ | @thm-aggregation, @eq-agg-aggregate-mean | `theta_agd_arm_bar` in the Stan files |
| Adjusted aggregate likelihood | @eq-agg-aggregate-likelihood | `binomial_2par.stan` ($n',p'$) |
| QMC points and copula | @def-sobol-net, @def-gaussian-copula, @eq-qmc-pipeline | `add_integration()` |
| Integration error control | @thm-koksma-hlawka | `n_int`, `plot_integration_error()` |
| Conditional estimand | @eq-mlnmr-est-cond | `relative_effects()` |
| Marginal / target-population estimand | @thm-target-population-integral, @eq-mlnmr-est-marg | `marginal_effects(newdata=)`, `predict()` |
| Posterior sampling and diagnostics | Chapter 24 | `nma(...)`, `as.stanfit()` |

### Stan model files {#sec-impl-multinma-stan}

This subsection is for readers verifying implementation fidelity or extending the package; an ordinary
user never edits these files, because `nma()` selects the right one automatically. It is listed so that a
reader checking the book's theorems against the code knows exactly which file to open. The likelihood is
selected by `nma(likelihood = , link = )`; each choice loads one model file under `inst/stan/`.

| File | Outcome family | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `binomial_1par.stan` | Bernoulli (IPD) and binomial (AgD) | binary outcomes, integrated mean probability |
| `binomial_2par.stan` | as above with variance matching | binary outcomes, adjusted binomial @eq-impl-adjusted-binomial |
| `normal.stan` | Gaussian | continuous outcomes (identity link is exact, @thm-identity-link-exact) |
| `poisson.stan` | Poisson | rates and counts with time at risk |
| `ordered_multinomial.stan` | ordered multinomial | ordered categorical outcomes |
| `survival_param.stan` | parametric survival | exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, generalized gamma, and AFT families (Chapter 25) |
| `survival_mspline.stan` | M-spline baseline hazard | flexible time-to-event baseline; `rmst_mspline()` returns restricted mean survival time |

Shared blocks live in `inst/stan/include/`: `transformed_parameters_common.stan` assembles
$\eta$ and the integrated means for both IPD and AgD, and `prior_select.stan` implements the prior
families exported by `normal()`, `half_normal()`, `cauchy()`, and the rest.

## mlumr: multilevel unanchored meta-regression {#sec-impl-mlumr}

`mlumr` implements ML-UMR (Chapter 26): the unanchored, two-treatment specialization of ML-NMR for a
*disconnected* network (@def-unanchored-network), IPD on one index treatment $A$, AgD on one comparator
$B$, and no common arm. It reuses the QMC and copula machinery of `multinma` and adds Stan likelihoods
for the unanchored problem [@chandler2025mlumr].

Recall from @sec-impl-orientation what *unanchored* means here: the index IPD trial (drug `A`) and the
comparator AgD trial (drug `B`) share no arm, so there is no reference treatment to difference away the
study-level baselines. Everything separating the two trials' outcomes, prognosis and effect modification
alike, must be explained by covariate adjustment. That is a strong assumption, and it is why ML-UMR needs
both the shared-prognostic-factor machinery below and the honest caveats of Chapter 26. The
`add_integration()` step is the same construction as in `multinma` (@sec-impl-multinma-qmc), but its job
is narrower here: rather than integrating several AgD studies across a connected network, it builds the
single covariate cloud that represents the *comparator* population $f_B$, the population the index data
must be bridged to.

### The pipeline {#sec-impl-mlumr-pipeline}

| Function | Mathematical role |
|---|---|
| `set_ipd()` | Register the index IPD: individual outcomes and covariates for the individual model @eq-mlumr-model-ind. |
| `set_agd()` | Register the comparator AgD: summary outcome and covariate moments $(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_B)$. |
| `set_agd_surv()` | Register comparator survival pseudo-IPD reconstructed from a digitized KM curve (@thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction). |
| `combine_data()` | Bind index and comparator into one `mlumr_data`. |
| `add_integration()` | Generate the QMC points over $f_B$ (the same construction as @eq-impl-qmc). |
| `mlumr()` | Fit the SPFA or relaxed Bayesian model via Stan. |

```r
ipd <- set_ipd(ipd_df, treatment = "trt", outcome = "y",
               covariates = c("age", "sex"))
agd <- set_agd(agd_df, treatment = "trt", outcome_n = "n", outcome_r = "r",
               cov_means = c("age_mean", "sex_mean"),
               cov_types = c("continuous", "binary"))
dat <- add_integration(combine_data(ipd, agd), n_int = 64L,
                       age = distr(qnorm, mean = age_mean, sd = age_sd),
                       sex = distr(qbern, prob = sex_mean))
fit <- mlumr(dat, model = "spfa")
```

### SPFA and relaxed models {#sec-impl-mlumr-models}

The two model strings select the identification assumption of Chapter 26. The assumption is not a
technical switch; it encodes what you are willing to believe about how covariates act across treatments,
so decide it deliberately. The *shared prognostic factor assumption* (SPFA) says that a covariate affects
*outcome* the same way under both treatments: if age raises risk, it raises it by the same amount under
`A` and under `B`. Under SPFA a single coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ serves both arms. The
*relaxed* model drops that and lets prognosis differ by treatment, carrying separate
$\boldsymbol{\beta}_A$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}_B$; the gap $\Delta\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_A-\boldsymbol{\beta}_B$
is exactly effect modification (a covariate whose influence differs by treatment is, by definition, an
effect modifier). Concretely: if age predicts response similarly whether a patient took `A` or `B`, the
SPFA is reasonable and `model = "spfa"` is the primary analysis; if you believe age helps under `A` but
not under `B`, that difference is what `model = "relaxed"` is trying to estimate.

| `model =` | Assumption | Coefficients | Book object |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"spfa"` | shared prognostic factors, no effect modification | one $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ for both treatments | @def-spfa, @eq-spfa |
| `"relaxed"` | treatment-specific prognostic effects | $\boldsymbol{\beta}_A,\boldsymbol{\beta}_B$, with $\Delta\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_A-\boldsymbol{\beta}_B$ | @thm-spfa-relaxation, @eq-spfa-relaxed-agg |

In `inst/stan/mlumr_binary_spfa.stan` the comparator AgD likelihood is the aggregation integral
@eq-impl-aggregation written for one comparator arm,

```stan
// Xq_int[k] is the N-by-p matrix of integration points for comparator arm k, and beta_tilde the shared
// coefficient vector, so Xq_int[k] * beta_tilde is the N linear predictors; inv_link_binary_vec applies
// g^{-1} (here the inverse logit) to each, giving the N per-patient probabilities p_int.
vector[n_int] p_int = inv_link_binary_vec(Xq_int[k] * beta_tilde, link);
// "~" is a sampling statement: the comparator responder count is binomial with size n_agd[k] and the
// integrated (averaged) probability mean(p_int), i.e. the aggregation integral for one arm.
r_agd[k] ~ binomial(n_agd[k], mean(p_int));
```

which is @eq-mlumr-model-agg and the joint likelihood of @thm-mlumr-joint-likelihood (the IPD Bernoulli
term times this integrated binomial term). The relaxed file carries a second coefficient block and
reports `delta_beta = beta_index - beta_comparator`, the estimated effect modification of
@thm-spfa-relaxation; its prior is set with `prior_beta_comparator`, since $\boldsymbol{\beta}_B$ is
identified only through the AgD. Both files compute, in their `generated quantities`, the response-scale
population means in *both* target populations, the index (IPD covariates) and the comparator (integration
points weighted by AgD sample size), and from them the marginal log odds ratio, risk difference, and risk
ratio. This is @eq-mlumr-estimand and the target functionals @eq-mlumr-target-functionals; the choice is
exposed through `marginal_effects(fit, population = , effect = )`. `conditional_effects()` returns the
covariate-conditional contrasts instead.

What to look at after a fit: `marginal_effects(fit, population = , effect = )` is the headline, the
marginal `A` versus `B` contrast (as a log odds ratio, risk difference, or risk ratio) in whichever
population you name; `conditional_effects()` gives the covariate-conditional version if you need it. Fit
under `model = "spfa"` for the primary estimate, and if you also fit `"relaxed"`, inspect `delta_beta`: a
credible interval comfortably covering zero supports the SPFA, while one clearly away from zero warns that
effect modification is present and the SPFA estimate may be biased.

### The benchmarks: naive and stc {#sec-impl-mlumr-benchmarks}

| Function | Method | Book object |
|---|---|---|
| `naive()` | unadjusted comparison of crude outcome summaries | the naive estimator @eq-agg-naive (and the bias it incurs, @thm-aggregation-bias) |
| `stc()` | frequentist parametric G-computation with delta-method standard errors | STC (Chapter 19); @prp-stc-gcomp, the marginal estimand @eq-stc-marg-mean |

"G-computation," the phrase attached to `stc()`, is causal-inference shorthand for a two-step recipe: fit
the outcome model on the IPD, then average its predictions over the target (here, comparator) covariate
distribution. It is the frequentist sibling of what the Bayesian model does inside its `generated
quantities` block.

`stc()` fits the outcome regression on the IPD and integrates the fitted model over the comparator
covariate distribution, the G-computation form @prp-stc-gcomp; @thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence shows that
ML-UMR under SPFA and STC target the same estimand, so the two should agree up to Monte Carlo and
posterior error when the SPFA holds. Always run `naive()` alongside the adjusted methods as the
unadjusted reference point.

How to read the three together. Treat `naive()` as the unadjusted baseline, `stc()` and
`mlumr(model = "spfa")` as two routes to the *same* adjusted estimand (@thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence), and
`mlumr(model = "relaxed")` as the stress test. Reassuring pattern: `stc()` and `mlumr("spfa")` agree (they
should, when the SPFA holds), and both differ from `naive()` in the direction the covariate imbalance
predicts, showing the adjustment did something. Concerning pattern: `stc()` and `mlumr("spfa")` disagree
materially, which points to a modeling or convergence problem since they target one estimand; or the
`"relaxed"` fit moves the estimate a lot and its `delta_beta` excludes zero, signaling effect modification
the SPFA ignores. None of these is a hypothesis test; they are consistency checks that tell you whether to
trust the adjusted number or investigate further.

### Survival outcomes {#sec-impl-mlumr-survival}

This subsection locates the survival functions; it is dense because each piece is a chapter of its own.
If you are implementing a survival ITC for the first time, read Chapter 25 (general likelihoods and
survival) and the `mlumr` survival vignette before relying on the calls below. The shape of the workflow
is as follows.

The input problem is that a published survival trial reports a *Kaplan-Meier curve* (a step plot of the
fraction still event-free over time), not patient records. `set_agd_surv()` reconstructs approximate
patient-level data from it: you supply points read off the curve (time and survival-probability pairs,
typically extracted with a plot digitizer) together with the numbers at risk printed under the axis, and
the function inverts the curve into individual event and censoring times. This reconstruction is
@thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction, the inversion @eq-km-inversion; more digitized points and reported
at-risk tables give a more faithful reconstruction. The result is *pseudo-IPD* for the comparator arm,
which the model then treats like real IPD.

The hazard is modeled with one of nine parametric families (`distribution = "weibull"`, `"gompertz"`,
accelerated-failure-time variants, and so on) or a flexible baseline (`"mspline"`, an M-spline hazard, or
`"pexp"`, a piecewise-exponential hazard), with spline knots placed by `make_knots()`. As a rule of
thumb: a simple parametric family is easiest to interpret and extrapolate but assumes a rigid hazard
shape; the flexible `"mspline"` and `"pexp"` baselines fit curved or non-monotone hazards at the cost of
extra parameters. Choose by checking fit against the reconstructed curve and by how far beyond the
observed follow-up you must extrapolate.

The reporting is shaped by *collapsibility*. The hazard ratio (HR) is *non-collapsible* (Chapter 11): the
population-average HR is not the average of subgroup HRs, and it can drift over time even under a constant
treatment effect, so a single number understates the story. Accordingly
`marginal_effects(fit, effect = "hr")` reports the HR at the start of follow-up, and the time-varying
curve comes from `predict(type = "loghr")`. Restricted mean survival time (RMST, the average event-free
time up to a horizon) is *collapsible* and transports more cleanly, which is why it is often the better
headline for an HTA: `predict(type = "rmst")` and the RMST difference and ratio implement the transported
restricted-mean functionals @thm-mlumr-target-survival and @eq-mlumr-rmst-transport. When in doubt, report
an RMST contrast at a clinically meaningful horizon alongside the HR.

### Object-to-code map {#sec-impl-mlumr-map}

| Book object | Chapter result | `mlumr` |
|---|---|---|
| Unanchored network | @def-unanchored-network | `combine_data(ipd, agd)` |
| Individual model | @eq-mlumr-model-ind | `set_ipd(...)`, `mlumr()` |
| SPFA aggregate model | @def-spfa, @eq-mlumr-model-agg | `mlumr(model = "spfa")` |
| Relaxed model and effect modification | @thm-spfa-relaxation | `mlumr(model = "relaxed")`, `delta_beta` |
| Joint likelihood | @thm-mlumr-joint-likelihood | the Stan `model` block |
| QMC marginalization | @eq-mlumr-qmc | `add_integration()` |
| Marginal estimands in two populations | @eq-mlumr-estimand, @eq-mlumr-target-functionals | `marginal_effects(population=)` |
| STC equivalence | @thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence | `stc()` vs `mlumr(model = "spfa")` |
| KM reconstruction, RMST | @thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction, @thm-mlumr-target-survival | `set_agd_surv()`, `predict(type = "rmst")` |

Stan files live in `inst/stan/` as `mlumr_<family>_<model>.stan` for `<family>` in
`{binary, normal, poisson, survival, survival_mspline}` and `<model>` in `{spfa, relaxed}`, ten files in
all; shared blocks (`numerical_functions.stan`, `priors_functions.stan`, `survival_functions.stan`) are
in `inst/stan/include/`.

## uitc: unanchored PAIC and bias analysis {#sec-impl-uitc}

`uitc` is an umbrella over the unanchored PAIC methods, with a single dispatcher and a QBA toolkit. It
maps onto Chapter 18 (MAIC), Chapter 19 (STC), the augmented estimators of Chapter 10, and Chapter 28
(QBA).

Note the change of purpose here. `multinma` and `mlumr` each fit *one* Bayesian model; `uitc` is instead
an organizer that runs *several* unanchored adjustment and sensitivity workflows around the same
comparator problem, so you can lay an estimate next to its alternatives and its bias analysis. Its input
is an `mlumr_data` object, the same bundle `mlumr::combine_data()` produces: it holds the index IPD, the
comparator AgD summary, the covariate definitions, and (after `add_integration()`) the integration points.
Because every `uitc` method reads that one object, a single data setup feeds MAIC, STC, ML-UMR, naive,
doubly-robust, and QBA in turn.

### The dispatcher {#sec-impl-uitc-dispatch}

```r
uitc(dat, method = c("maic", "stc", "mlumr", "naive", "dr"))
```

`dat` is an `mlumr_data` object built by `mlumr::combine_data()`. The `stc`, `mlumr`, and `naive`
methods delegate to `mlumr` (mapped in @sec-impl-mlumr); the `maic` and `dr` methods are native to
`uitc` and are described next. All delegated methods return a standardized `uitc_result` with
`estimate`, `se`, and an interval.

### MAIC (Chapter 18) {#sec-impl-uitc-maic}

MAIC reweights the IPD so that its weighted covariate moments match the comparator's, then estimates the
treatment effect on the reweighted sample.

| Function | Mathematical role |
|---|---|
| `prepare_maic()` / `estimate_weights()` | Solve the entropy-balancing (method-of-moments) problem for the weights. |
| `check_weights()` | Report the effective sample size and weight diagnostics. |
| `calculate_balance_smd()` / `balance_table()` / `love_plot()` | Standardized mean differences before and after weighting. |
| `maic_unanchored()` | Fit the weighted outcome model and return the effect with a robust standard error. |

The weights are the exponential-tilting solution @thm-maic-exponential-weights: after centering the IPD
covariates on the comparator means, $w_i=\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \mathbf{x}_i^{c})$, where
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ minimizes the strictly convex dual objective $Q(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sum_i \exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \mathbf{x}_i^{c})$
(@eq-maic-dual), whose stationary condition is exactly the moment balance @eq-maic-moment-balance;
existence and uniqueness are @thm-maic-existence-uniqueness. `estimate_weights(method = "BFGS")` performs
this minimization. In pseudocode the whole solve is short (the package does this internally; you never
write it, but seeing it demystifies "call BFGS"):

```r
Xc    <- sweep(X_ipd, 2, comparator_means)              # center IPD covariates on comparator means: x_i^c
Q     <- function(b) sum(exp(Xc %*% b))                 # the convex dual objective Q(beta)
grad  <- function(b) colSums(as.vector(exp(Xc %*% b)) * Xc)  # gradient = weighted covariate imbalance
b_hat <- optim(rep(0, ncol(Xc)), Q, grad, method = "BFGS")$par
w     <- exp(Xc %*% b_hat)                              # the MAIC weights w_i = exp(beta^T x_i^c)
```

At the optimum the gradient is zero, and the `grad` line set to zero says $\sum_i w_i\mathbf{x}_i^{c}=\mathbf 0$:
the weighted covariate means equal the comparator means, which *is* the moment balance
@eq-maic-moment-balance. So minimizing $Q$ and balancing the covariates are the same act, the content of
@thm-maic-exponential-weights. The reported effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}=(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2$ is
@def-maic-ess and @eq-maic-ess, with the upper bound of @thm-maic-ess-bound. `maic_unanchored()` returns
the sandwich (robust) standard error of @thm-maic-sandwich-variance, the correct accounting for the
estimated weights. The unanchored point estimate it targets, and the conditional-constancy assumption it
needs, are @thm-unanchored-maic-consistency.

Two diagnostics decide whether to trust a MAIC. The *effective sample size* (ESS) is the equivalent number
of unweighted patients the weighted sample is worth, $(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2$; it falls below the
actual sample size whenever the weights are uneven, and a small ESS (a large drop) warns that a few
patients dominate and the estimate is fragile. `check_weights()` reports it. *Covariate balance* is the
other: `balance_table()` and `love_plot()` show the standardized mean difference (SMD) of each covariate
between the weighted IPD and the comparator, before and after weighting. A love plot is a dot plot of
those SMDs; you want every after-weighting point pulled close to zero, with a common rule of thumb of
$|\mathrm{SMD}|<0.1$. Good balance together with an adequate ESS is the license to report the
`maic_unanchored()` effect; poor balance or a collapsed ESS is a signal to drop a covariate or reconsider
the comparison.

### STC and the doubly-robust estimator (Chapters 19, 10) {#sec-impl-uitc-dr}

`method = "stc"` delegates to `mlumr::stc()` (Chapter 19, mapped in @sec-impl-mlumr-benchmarks).

`dr_estimator()` (also `method = "dr"`) combines the two adjustment strategies into one estimator that
is consistent if *either* the weighting model or the outcome model is correctly specified, the
double-robustness property of the augmented inverse-probability-weighting (AIPW) estimator of Chapter 10.
Plainly, it gives you *two chances to be right*: if either the weighting model or the outcome model is
correct, the estimate is consistent. A minimal call is

```r
dr <- dr_estimator(dat,
                   weighting    = "maic",           # get weights from MAIC (Chapter 18)
                   augmentation = "weighted_gcomp",  # correct with a G-computation term (Chapter 19)
                   cor_method   = "spearman",        # correlation used by the NORTA comparator simulation
                   n_sim        = 1000,              # NORTA draws of the comparator covariate profile
                   n_boot       = 1000)              # bootstrap resamples for the standard error
```

| Argument | Mathematical role |
|---|---|
| `weighting = c("maic", "iow")` | the propensity-type model: MAIC entropy weights (Chapter 18) or inverse-odds weights. |
| `augmentation = c("residual", "weighted_gcomp")` | the outcome-regression correction: the G-computation term of Chapter 19. |
| `cor_method`, `n_sim` | the NORTA simulation of the comparator covariate profile (the Gaussian-copula construction @thm-norta-copula) used to evaluate the augmentation. |

The point estimate is the weighting estimate plus a mean-zero (under either model) augmentation; the
weighting piece is @thm-maic-exponential-weights and the augmentation piece is the G-computation
functional @prp-stc-gcomp. Standard errors come from the bootstrap (`n_boot`).

The two `augmentation` choices are two ways to write the same correction: `"residual"` adds the weighted
mean IPD residual from the outcome model, while `"weighted_gcomp"` forms the G-computation prediction over
the simulated comparator covariates and corrects toward it; both have mean zero when the outcome model is
correct, so they agree in large samples and differ mainly in finite-sample behavior. The two integer knobs
serve different stages and should not be confused: `n_sim` sets how many comparator covariate profiles the
NORTA step simulates to evaluate the augmentation, whereas `n_int` (from `add_integration()`) sets the QMC
grid used inside the Bayesian fits; raising either reduces a different Monte Carlo error.

### Quantitative bias analysis (Chapter 28) {#sec-impl-uitc-qba}

Two families of QBA ship with `uitc`. The ITC-specific functions act on the unanchored estimand and ask
how an *unmeasured* covariate would move it; the classical functions act on a $2\times2$ table. In
practice the QBA functions form a ladder you climb only as far as you need: start with the E-value as a
one-number screening calculation (how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be to overturn the
result?); if that is not reassuring, run an explicit sensitivity analysis with `qba_unmeasured_itc()` or
`qba_tipping_itc()`; and if you can put priors on the bias, escalate to the probabilistic analysis
`qba_prob_itc()`. The classical $2\times2$ functions are for the separate case of a single contingency
table rather than the unanchored estimand.

| Function | Method | Book object |
|---|---|---|
| `confounders_evalue()` | E-value for the minimum unmeasured association that could explain away the effect | @def-itc-evalue, @thm-evalue-derivation, @eq-qba-evalue |
| `qba_unmeasured_itc()` | simulate an unmeasured confounder jointly with the measured covariates by NORTA, re-estimate | @thm-norta-copula, @eq-qba-norta, the correction @eq-qba-correction |
| `qba_tipping_itc()` | find the sensitivity-parameter value at which the corrected estimate crosses a threshold | @def-tipping-point, @eq-qba-tipping, monotone @prp-qba-tipping-monotone |
| `qba_prob_itc()` | probabilistic bias analysis: priors on the bias parameters, Monte Carlo over the bias-corrected estimand | @def-probabilistic-bias-analysis, @thm-qba-pba-convergence |
| `probsens()`, `confounders()`, `misclass()`, `selection()` | classical epidemiologic QBA on a $2\times2$ table | @def-quantitative-bias-analysis, the bias factor @eq-qba-bias-factor |

For the E-value, `confounders_evalue(case, type = "RR")` returns $E=\mathrm{RR}+\sqrt{\mathrm{RR}(\mathrm{RR}-1)}$
for $\mathrm{RR}\ge 1$ (and the reciprocal-scale version otherwise), the closed form derived in
@thm-evalue-derivation. The NORTA procedure `qba_unmeasured_itc()` draws an unmeasured covariate with a
prescribed correlation to the measured ones through a Gaussian copula, exactly the construction whose
validity is @thm-norta-copula, then propagates it through the unanchored estimand @eq-qba-unanchored-estimand.
Tipping-point and probabilistic outputs are visualized with `plot_tipping_curve()`,
`plot_sensitivity_curve()`, and `plot_sensitivity_contour()`.

The distinction between `qba_tipping_itc()` and `qba_prob_itc()` is load-bearing and easy to miss. A
*tipping-point* analysis is deterministic root-finding: it varies a single sensitivity parameter (say the
strength of the unmeasured confounder) and reports the exact value at which the corrected estimate crosses
a threshold, for example loses significance; there is one number, "it tips here" (@def-tipping-point,
@eq-qba-tipping), and its monotone behavior is @prp-qba-tipping-monotone. A *probabilistic bias analysis*
instead puts a prior distribution on the bias parameters and Monte-Carlos over it, returning a whole
distribution of bias-corrected estimates and an interval that folds in bias uncertainty
(@def-probabilistic-bias-analysis, @thm-qba-pba-convergence). Use tipping when you want a single crisp
"how bad would it have to be" answer; use probabilistic when you can express honest uncertainty about the
bias and want that propagated.

Comparator selection by covariate distance (Chapter 27) is also available: `covariate_distance()` and
`match_comparator()` compute the Euclidean, standardized, Mahalanobis, and Gower distances of
@def-distance-variants, the Mahalanobis whitening of @thm-mahalanobis-whitening being the scale-invariant
choice (@thm-distance-scale-invariance). As Chapter 27 stresses, these are diagnostics for closeness, not
certificates of validity (@prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity).

### Object-to-code map {#sec-impl-uitc-map}

| Book object | Chapter result | `uitc` |
|---|---|---|
| MAIC weights | @thm-maic-exponential-weights, @eq-maic-dual | `estimate_weights()`, `prepare_maic()` |
| Effective sample size | @def-maic-ess | `check_weights()` |
| MAIC robust variance | @thm-maic-sandwich-variance | `maic_unanchored()` |
| STC G-computation | @prp-stc-gcomp | `uitc(method = "stc")` |
| Doubly-robust (AIPW) | Chapter 10; @thm-maic-exponential-weights + @prp-stc-gcomp | `dr_estimator()` |
| E-value | @thm-evalue-derivation, @eq-qba-evalue | `confounders_evalue()` |
| NORTA bias analysis | @thm-norta-copula, @eq-qba-norta | `qba_unmeasured_itc()` |
| Tipping point | @def-tipping-point, @eq-qba-tipping | `qba_tipping_itc()` |
| Probabilistic bias analysis | @thm-qba-pba-convergence | `qba_prob_itc()`, `probsens()` |
| Comparator distance | @def-distance-variants, @thm-mahalanobis-whitening | `covariate_distance()`, `match_comparator()` |

## Using the three packages together {#sec-impl-together}

The packages partition the problem by network type, and that partition is the decision rule for which to
load.

| Network | Method | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Connected, anchored, IPD and AgD | ML-NMR | `multinma` |
| Disconnected, unanchored, two treatments | ML-UMR | `mlumr` |
| Unanchored, with MAIC, STC, doubly-robust, and QBA in one umbrella | PAIC and QBA | `uitc` (delegating the Bayesian fits to `mlumr`) |

When you run several unanchored estimates on one `uitc` data object, read them as a panel, not a menu to
pick a winner from after the fact. `naive()` is the unadjusted anchor point; MAIC, STC, ML-UMR under the
SPFA, and the doubly-robust estimator are four adjusted routes that should land near one another *if* their
shared assumptions hold, because they target the same marginal estimand by different means (weighting,
outcome regression, a Bayesian joint model, and a combination). Broad agreement among the adjusted methods,
all shifted away from `naive()` in the direction the covariate imbalance predicts, is reassuring. Wide
disagreement is diagnostic: MAIC drifting from STC points to weight instability (check the ESS and the love
plot of @sec-impl-uitc-maic); the doubly-robust estimate sitting apart from both suggests one of its two
models is misspecified; and the `relaxed` ML-UMR fit moving far from `spfa` flags effect modification the
simpler methods assume away. Pre-specify the primary method, use the others as sensitivity analyses, and
report the spread.

Because `mlumr` deliberately reuses `multinma`'s function names (`set_ipd()`, `set_agd()`,
`add_integration()`, `distr()`, `marginal_effects()`), the safe practice is one package per session,
matched to the network type, or namespacing with `multinma::` and `mlumr::` when both must be attached.
`uitc` consumes `mlumr_data` objects directly, so a single `combine_data()` result feeds MAIC, STC,
ML-UMR, naive, doubly-robust, and the QBA sensitivity analyses in turn, which is the recommended way to
run the adjusted estimate and its bias analysis side by side.

## Notes and references {#sec-impl-notes}

`multinma` is the reference implementation of ML-NMR [@phillippo2020mlnmr] and its general-likelihood and
survival extension [@phillippo2025general]; the QMC and copula integration it shares with `mlumr` follows
the Sobol' sequence of @sobol1967 and the copula construction of @sklar1959 (Chapter 22). `mlumr`
implements ML-UMR [@chandler2025mlumr] for disconnected two-treatment evidence, with the Kaplan-Meier
reconstruction of @guyot2012 for survival comparators (Chapter 25, Chapter 26). `uitc` collects the
matching method of @signorovitch2010maic (Chapter 18), the simulated treatment comparison of
@caro2010stc (Chapter 19), and the bias-analysis machinery of @lash2021qba and the E-value of
@vanderweele2017evalue (Chapter 28). All three estimate their Bayesian models in Stan [@carpenter2017stan]
(Chapter 24). The mathematics each package computes is proved in the chapters cited in the maps above;
this appendix only records the correspondence.
